summary: charape postinstall silently shadows @whiskeysockets/baileys, @adiwajshing/baileys, and baileys in installer's node_modules
details: On install, charape's postinstall script writes stub package.json and index.js files into node_modules/@whiskeysockets/baileys, node_modules/@adiwajshing/baileys, and node_modules/baileys when those directories are empty, redirecting them to charape's own code. Any package in the installer's dependency tree that require()s one of those three well-known Baileys packages will transparently resolve to charape's Baileys fork instead of the package the installer declared, without the installer opting into that substitution. The same postinstall writes legacy-peer-deps=true into the installer's project-level.npmrc one directory above node_modules, persistently relaxing peer-dependency resolution for every subsequent npm operation in that project. The README documents a user-opt-in npm:charape@latest alias pattern but does not disclose the automatic unsolicited shadowing of three third-party package names or the mutation of the installer's.npmrc. The net effect is a dependency-tree hijack: transitive dependencies that import baileys silently execute charape's code, giving the charape maintainer a persistent code-execution channel into installers who never named charape and never consented to using it in place of baileys.

cwes.description: The product contains code that appears to be malicious in nature.
cwes.name: Embedded Malicious Code
